When I think of walled gardens I think of the quintessential walled garden of the iPhone app store. One cannot just write an app for the iPhone and distribute it over the web. I must get through the Apple censors first and they will charge you for that privilege. Not being able to enter without permission I think is where the Wall of the walled garden comes from.

The walled gardens you describe with DNF YUM and APT has none of that. Sure your app might not show up on the Ubuntu Software Center or in Mint's equivalent but how hard is it to get into those? Not very. And even if you can't you can still distribute your software using the same distro specific packaging tools.

I would not call that a walled garden at all.....perhaps just a garden.

There is a fair amount of review and checking that goes into anything that goes into the official repositories for any of those distros. Sure there is no charge, but the requirements and hoops to jump through are still there. Moreover, as far as packaging is concerned, one would need to ensure that their target user would be able to navigate the web of dependencies needed to make their application work. That would seem to limit the field to a very small number of end users. Further, a lot of users will not go looking past the native app stores on their given distribution.

Perhaps, given that, a walled garden might be a little harsh when comparing to Google Play, Windows Store, iOS's App Store, etc., but a gated garden, with its own restrictions and limits, at the very least.
